description: We’re a team passionate about AI, robotics, mathematics, and space exploration. We have experience in programming, engineering, and problem-solving. We’re looking for creative teammates with skills in coding, design, data analysis, or science who are excited to collaborate and build something innovative for NASA Space Apps!
summary: Interstellar Sonata lets you listen to our changing planet. NASA publishes amazing Earth visualizations showing ocean currents, aerosol plumes, and rainfall patterns. These images are beautiful, but they only reach people through sight. Our app does something different. It takes those same NASA visualizations and turns them into sound created right in real time. Brightness becomes pitch. Color becomes your instrument choice. And when things change over time, that drives the rhythm. Pick two regions of NASA's ocean current data, aerosol patterns, or precipitation data and compare them side by side. Instead of hunting for the differences in the pictures, you hear them. This matters for people who can't see images. It matters for people who learn better by listening. Now everyone can follow the same evidence. Interstellar Sonata gives people more than one sense to understand our planet, so it doesn't matter if you're sighted or not.
details:
Earth Sonata: Play the Planet

The big idea

NASA's pictures of Earth are made to be looked at. That leaves out anyone who can't see the screen, and even sighted people can miss a pattern hiding in the swirls.

Earth Sonata turns those pictures into rhythm. You pick a picture, pick a circle on it, and press Play. If the lines in the circle mostly run the same way, you hear an even, steady pulse. If they run every which way, you hear a lopsided one: a long gap, then a short gap. Switch to another circle and the beat carries on from the same moment, so you can hear the difference between two places in a few seconds.

It's also a small instrument. You can play your own melody on top of the Earth rhythm, or let a line sweep across the whole picture and play whatever colour it crosses.

Three honest things first:

  • It is a visualization of computer model output (ECCO2 for the ocean currents, GEOS for the aerosols) or of satellite estimates (IMERG for the rain). It is not a photo.
  • The rhythm rule is a choice we made. Nature doesn't say "even pulse". We did.
  • The sound describes the drawn picture. It does not tell you water speed, turbulence, air quality or how much rain fell.

Try it

In a hurry? Open the app on Listen and press Play. Then tap the other circle on the picture. The rhythm changes on the next beat, with no restart.

Five tabs run along the top: Listen, Compare, How it's made, Play along and Globe. On tablets and phones, below 1024 pixels wide, they move to a bar along the bottom. A sixth link, Game, opens a separate listening game page. Changing tab stops all sound, the back button works between tabs, and there is a light and dark switch.

Listen.

Nothing plays until you press Play. First choose a picture (Ocean, Aerosols or Rain). Then choose a region: tap a circle on the picture, use the round thumbnails, or use the arrow keys on the region choice (1 and 2 work there too). Press Play and the region plays one beat a second, two pulses a beat. A beat lane lights each pulse as it sounds, with the date under the first beat of each day. Pause, Stop, Replay and a Sound panel (speed from ½× to 1¼×, and volume) sit beside it. Esc stops everything from anywhere.

Press Explain for one plain sentence about the beat you are hearing, such as "Region A's lines point every which way, so its second pulse comes late. Alignment is 0.08." It also shows both circles with the beat each one makes. For screen readers, the full sentence also says how the region compares with the other one at the same moment.

Compare.

Each circle gets a close up, with short ticks showing which way the lines run there. A big number shows the alignment, thin when swirly and heavy when lined up, next to a word (Lined up, Partly lined up or Swirly) and where the second pulse falls. Each circle has its own Listen button and a row showing its rhythm. Below that, both rhythms share one timeline, with a small table of the numbers and curves of alignment over the frames.

How it's made.

Three small pictures with a line each: a circle on the NASA picture, which way the lines run, and how agreement sets the rhythm. Under them: the rule in one line, the three honest lines from above, and a credit for each of the three pictures.

Play along.

Three things live here: Play the picture, Your melody and Test your ear. They are described below.

Globe.

The picture you chose, wrapped on a 3D globe. Drag it or use the arrow keys to turn it, and use the wheel, a pinch or the zoom buttons to zoom. Press "Play Region A" and the globe turns to that circle, which shows as a brighter patch, and plays it. The same button becomes Stop.

[IMAGE 5: The Globe tab turned to a region, with the Play Region buttons visible | take a new screenshot]

How a picture becomes sound

First in plain English.

Each NASA picture is drawn with thin lines: currents, plumes of particles, bands of rain. We put a circle on a region and ask one question about the lines inside it. Do they mostly run the same way, or every which way?

The answer is a number from 0 (every which way) to 1 (all the same way). We call it alignment.

Each frame of the picture becomes one beat of one second, made of two short pulses. The more the lines line up, the more evenly the two pulses are spaced. Everything else stays fixed: tempo, pitch, loudness and the length of each pulse. So timing is the only thing to listen for.

Now the rule. The second pulse lands at 0.75 minus 0.25 times the alignment, as a share of the beat.

  • Alignment 1: the second pulse lands halfway. An even beat.
  • Alignment 0.5: about 62 to 38. A slight lilt.
  • Alignment 0: three quarters of the way. A long gap, then a short one. We call this long then short.

The two gaps always add up to one beat, so the tempo never moves.

How the number is measured. We do this ahead of time in Python, with NumPy and OpenCV. Every bit of visible line votes with an arrow along its direction, and stronger lines get longer arrows. We double the angles first, because a line at 10 degrees and a line at 190 degrees are the same line. Add the arrows up. If the lines run the same way, the total is long and the alignment is near 1. If they run every which way, the arrows cancel and it is near 0.

Land is left out. A frame where fewer than 5% of the circle's pixels show a clear line is marked missing, with a reason, and is never given a number. The Earth voice goes quiet and the app says why. The alignments are lightly smoothed from frame to frame and saved as checked files. In your browser, every sound is made live by our own code with Tone.js.

The three NASA pictures

You choose the picture on Listen, Compare or Globe. Each picture is measured with its own settings, and numbers are never compared between pictures. That is a rule from Developer A. Regions are lettered A and B (Ocean), C and D (Aerosols) and E and F (Rain).

Ocean: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature (NASA SVS 3912).

Ocean surface currents computed by the ECCO2 model and drawn as flow lines, coloured by modelled sea surface temperature. It is part of NASA's Earth Information Center collection. We use 30 frames from 25 to 30 March 2007 model time, about four hours apart, so the 30 second loop covers about five days.

  • Region A, the Kuroshio eddies east of Japan: lines run in many directions. Average alignment 0.072, second pulse about 73% of the way through the beat.
  • Region B, streaks in the Equatorial Pacific: lines partly line up. Average alignment 0.672, second pulse about 58%.
  • At the same moment the two second pulses land about 150 milliseconds apart. Both circles measured cleanly in all 30 frames.

Aerosols: GEOS Aerosols (NASA SVS 5669).

A GEOS model picture of tiny particles in the air. Colours show the kind: blue for sea salt, pink for dust, orange and red for smoke, green for sulfates. It is one still picture, for 19 August 2025 at 20:00 UTC, so nothing changes over time and each region plays the same one second beat again and again. It comes from the challenge's resource list rather than the Earth Information Center gallery.

  • Region C, sulfate and sea salt streaks near Vanuatu: alignment 0.53, second pulse about 62%.
  • Region D, sea salt cells in the southeast Pacific: alignment 0.015, second pulse about 75%.
  • About 130 milliseconds apart.

Rain: Near Real Time Global Precipitation (NASA SVS 4285).

Rain estimates from the GPM IMERG satellites, also in the Earth Information Center collection. We use 30 hourly frames, from 00:00 UTC on 14 November to 05:00 UTC on 15 November 2026. NASA keeps only about the latest week of these frames, so we saved our own copy.

  • Region E, a long rain band in the South Pacific: average alignment 0.324, second pulse about 67%.
  • Region F, scattered showers on the equator in the central Pacific: average alignment 0.077, second pulse about 73%.
  • About 60 milliseconds apart. That is a smaller difference than the ocean's, and both regions lean long then short.

On the real pictures nothing reaches a perfectly even beat. The ocean streaks and the Vanuatu streaks come closest, with a slight lilt.

Credits: Ocean, NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio. Aerosols, NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office and Scientific Visualization Studio. Rain, NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio.

Play the picture and your melody

These are extras on the Play along tab. They are not part of the rhythm rule, and neither can change an Earth note. A browser test checks that.

Play the picture.

A line sweeps the NASA ocean picture from west to east in 30 seconds. Or choose Region A or B and a radar line turns once around the circle in 15 seconds. As the line crosses colour, you hear:

  • Height on the map, or distance from the centre for the radar, sets the pitch. There are twelve notes from C3 to C6, all from the C major pentatonic scale, so nothing clashes.
  • How strong the colour is sets how loud that height sounds.
  • Each height is held as a soft choir note, and a low note underneath swells with the colour on the whole line.
  • A peak of colour strikes one chime. The red side of yellow strikes a marimba. The rest strike bells.

The picture lights up as the line passes, and each chime leaves a mark. A legend names every mark. You can choose between three sounds: Ocean choir, Music box and Plain. We build all of them in code, with no recordings. The bells and the music box get their tones from the equations of a vibrating bar.

The method follows NASA's own image sonifications by the SYSTEM Sounds team: a line or radar sweeps the picture, position sets pitch, light sets loudness and colour picks the instrument. [CHECK: docs/DECISIONS.md tags sources S9 to S11 as Verified, but says an AI research assistant fetched and quoted them and Developer A had not yet read them.]

We tag every claim about it, in docs/mapping_spec.md:

  • Verified: the Earth rhythm does not change while the scan plays (a browser test). Louder colour gives a louder sound: in recordings each doubling of the level raised that tone by about 6 decibels. Black sea and grey land are silent on the ocean picture. The held notes never clash with each other. The bar tones match the equations (a test solves them again).
  • Design choice: pitch as height, loudness as colour strength, which colours strike which instrument, and the chime rule, which leaves out 39% to 61% of colour peaks.
  • Unverified: that it sounds good, and that anyone can hear a region's character in it. One listener, Developer A, has heard the first two versions. The third round has been measured, not heard. Nobody has tested it.

Loudness follows colour strength, not current speed. Warm colours are drawn stronger than cold ones, so warm lines are louder. It plays the ocean picture only, because the aerosol and rain pictures failed its checks: rain's dark blue sea would sound in every cell, and aerosol sea sounds in 93% of sea cells.

Your melody.

Tab to the melody keys and play A S D F G H J K, or click the on screen keys. The eight keys use the same five note scale as the picture scan, so whatever you play fits. Choose from six sounds: Glass keys, Marimba, Bells, Music box, Choir pad and the plain first tone. Letter keys only play while the keys have focus, so they don't clash with screen readers or speech input. The Earth rhythm, the scan and your melody each have their own volume, and Stop or Esc silences all three.

Test your ear.

The Game link opens a separate practice page. You hear a mystery rhythm and pick which of two patches of the NASA picture made it. We set the pass mark before anyone listened: 9 of 10 correct, which guessing reaches about 1 time in 100.

Who it helps

  • People who can't see the screen. They can compare two parts of a NASA picture by ear, using only a keyboard, and hear the difference explained in words. We built it for that. We have not yet tested it with a blind or low vision listener, as the limits below say.
  • Sighted visitors. A pattern that is easy to miss by eye becomes a timing to listen for, with the picture and the close ups beside it.
  • Anyone curious, including classrooms. Every sound can be traced back to its NASA frame, its date, its circle and the number that made it. Nothing is hidden inside a trained model. It shows how a scientific picture becomes numbers, and why each choice along the way matters.

Our hope is that the pictures in NASA's Earth Information Center reach people who can't see them, and that anyone can explore them by ear. Earth Sonata is a small, honest template for that: one measured property of the picture, one property of the sound, a rule in plain words, and tests that check the sound matches the numbers. The same steps (check the source, choose regions, measure, play, explain) have already prepared and measured regions in two more NASA pictures, GEOS aerosols and GPM IMERG rain, so the method is not tied to one image.

It runs in a web browser with no sign in, no installation and no outside service to make sound. The app's own code calls no outside service. [CHECK: this comes from searching the code and a local test on 14 November. docs/dev_b_checks.md still lists a real wifi off run of the final build as to do, so do not say it works offline.]

What makes it creative

  • The data is in the rhythm, not the pitch. Where the second of two pulses lands carries the measurement. Tempo, pitch, loudness and note length stay fixed, so a listener follows one thing.
  • Data and music play together. The Earth rhythm is the data, and you play your own melody on top. A browser test checks that the melody never changes the Earth rhythm.
  • A line that plays the picture. A sweep or a radar turns colour into chimes, and the picture lights up as it sounds.
  • Instruments from physics. We tuned the bells and the music box by solving the equations of a vibrating bar.
  • The sound explains itself. At any beat, the app can say in words which number made the sound and how two regions compare.
  • Listening becomes a game. Hear a rhythm, pick the patch that made it, and find out whether the difference can really be heard.
  • Play a region from the globe. Turn the planet to a circle and press Play.
